stories.title: Proton's CTO tells engineers "Your old job is gone": the job is now directing AI agents, and the next step is rebuilding the whole development process
stories.one_liner: Proton published an internal memo by CTO Bart Butler arguing that writing code by hand is no longer the engineer's core job.
stories.summary: Proton published an internal memo by CTO Bart Butler, written about a month earlier for its engineers. It says writing great code manually is "a core skill whose time has passed" and that every engineer is now "a team leader, a manager" whose direct reports are the models and agents they use: their job is to help the LLM write better code faster, step in where it cannot, and improve shared context files, skills and prompts so it needs less babysitting. Butler stresses this is "not the death of expertise" nor of good engineering practices, though some rules, such as how many tests are worth writing, will change as costs fall. He says Proton has been stuck in "phase 1", using LLMs to speed up existing workflows, which is why productivity has not jumped; "phase 2" means removing the bottlenecks that appear elsewhere, such as CI, design, approvals and code review, and he expects most human code review to end. He calls falling behind "an existential threat to the success of the mission itself" and says it is past time for Proton to commit as an organisation.

stories.title: OpenAI research: training choices make frontier models' reasoning harder to monitor
stories.one_liner: OpenAI's safety team says four training steps, including architecture and reinforcement learning, make GPT-6 Astra's chains of thought harder to monitor, and that this is tied to capability and cost.
stories.summary: OpenAI's safety team studied models from GPT-5 through GPT-6 Astra to find why chains of thought are harder for monitors to read. It traced the problem to four main causes across the training cycle. Silent reasoning without a scratchpad rises with base model capability. One of three anonymized architectures, "Architecture 2", favored silent multi-step reasoning. Reinforcement learning now increases control over the reasoning log in Astra-class and internal "Terra" models. Student models inherit a teacher's high CoT controllability. OpenAI says the loss of transparency is not purely a law of nature. A smaller model that reasons at greater length can be easier to monitor, but it raises compute costs.
stories.eli5: Imagine a kid who used to say each math step out loud, so the teacher could follow along. Now the kid does the steps quietly in their head, and the teacher can't see how they got the answer.

stories.title: AIE Code Summit 2026 speakers and attendees publish 'No AI Slop' manifesto
stories.one_liner: Speakers and attendees of AIE Code Summit 2026 wrote a manifesto saying people must own the quality of AI output and not pass on unreviewed work.
stories.summary: Speakers and attendees of AIE Code Summit 2026 published the No AI Slop manifesto. It is modeled on the 2001 Agile Manifesto. It lists five values, including outcomes over output and understanding over speed. It defines slop as putting less effort into producing something than the consumer must spend understanding it. It says using AI does not by itself make something slop. It resolves that people own what they ship, say when an agent wrote it, and review at least some output, depending on the stakes. It also says anything a linter or type checker can catch should be left to it. Signatures are collected through gist comments.

stories.title: Perplexity releases Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 decision models
stories.one_liner: Perplexity released Decider v1.3 and a smaller Flash version, general-purpose classifiers that return probabilities and add a new locate feature for extracting text.
stories.summary: Perplexity released Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, a smaller model distilled from Decider v1.3. Both are on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API. A decision model takes an input and several questions, then returns a probability distribution over answers in a single forward pass. It handles Yes/No, multiple choice and score questions. Version 1.3 uses bidirectional attention, better-curated training data and a refined training recipe. It also adds locate, which returns exact matching text from the input with start and end character positions, for tasks like named entity recognition and extractive question answering.
